# Alex Frank

Dan's cousin — described by Dan as "semi-famous" — and, per public
sources, a real working journalist and editor based in Brooklyn covering
music, fashion, and culture. He was Deputy Editor at The FADER and Deputy
Culture Editor at Vogue.com, and has bylined at Vogue, The FADER,
Pitchfork, ELLE, Dazed & Confused, New York Magazine, Vulture, Fantastic
Man, the Village Voice, GQ, V Man, and The New York Times Style Magazine,
with celebrity profiles and interviews spanning Aretha Franklin, Bjork,
Tyler the Creator, Andre 3000, SZA, Young Thug, Kacey Musgraves, Virgil
Abloh, RuPaul, and many others.

The connection to Dan runs through the paternal Frank line: Dan's
grandfather and Alex's grandfather were **brothers**. That makes Alex Dan's
cousin (first cousin once removed) and puts [[wiki/people/morley-frank|Morley Jay Frank]] — Alex's
"Uncle Morley" — as the shared great-uncle on the paternal side. The
Frank-family funeral in Alex's essay is family material to Dan, not
distant gossip.

## Alex's first-person account

Alex's own first-person essay account of the Morley funeral cookie story —
quoted verbatim:

> I always tell this story about my Uncle Morley. He was a real pisser, you know? You might have an Uncle Morley in your family, but this guy made the mold. His humor was a mix of self-deprecation, sexual harassment, and insult, but his endearing, crooked half-smile (my Grandpa had the exact same grin) kept the smart, well-humored ones from being too hurt by his jokes. I was too young to quite get it, but I did get a sense of no-bullshit from him that children always respond to. Anyway, there's this diner in Pittsburgh, Eat'n Park that's famous for making frosted smily face cookies. They've been doing it for decades, and they're one of those Pittsburgh symbols that unite us (The Original, Primanti's sandwiches, Mineo's: they're all food, of course, we're fat, okay?). Anyway, everyday Uncle Morley stopped at the Eat'n Park by his house for a coffee, stared at the shelves and shelves of Eat'n Park cookies mocking him with their smiles and asked the cashier one thing: "I'm having a shit day, can't you be fair and make me a frownie face cookie?" They laughed off his self-deprecating routine like anyone would. But he asked everyday. And they never gave it to him.
>
> When Uncle Morley died, his wife Sis had boxes of frownie face cookies made up from the local Eat'n Park for his funeral party. When we all walked in and saw the inverted symbol strewn amongst the more generic catered items, it expressed a certain kind of familial understanding that comes from generations of genetic personality traits, like a fucked up sense of humor and melancholy lense on life. The more earnest funeral goers didn't get the joke, I suspect. But the smart, well-humored ones did. And they're the only ones you want at the party anyway.

## Source material & corroboration

The behavioral corpus shows Dan keeps returning to Alex's byline and
career rather than to Alex the person — an "involuntary search-history"
pattern the dossiers read as ordinary proud-cousin interest. From
`raw/self/dox-scan/browser_history_analysis.txt`:

- **Alex Frank — 29 search hits total**, with a notable **2025 cluster of
  10** around the queries "alex frank mac miller / gq / malcolm." The
  analysis frames Alex as the **"sincere-enthusiast pole"** cousin — the
  inverse of the ex-partners, who appear mainly as retrospective forensic
  subjects — and reads the 2025 timing as a **recent re-engagement with a
  developmental-origin thread** (Alex's Mac Miller / GQ / Malcolm
  Gladwell-adjacent culture work).

Dan also re-tells the frownie-cookie story himself, independently of
Alex's essay, which confirms it as a live family reference rather than a
single published anecdote. From `raw/self/dox-md/LIFE_EVENTS_CALENDAR.md`,
logged **2025-09-03**:

> eat n' park delivered frownie cookies to my granfather's funeral i swear to god lmao

(The "grandfather" here is Morley — the funeral Alex's essay documents.)
That Dan is still surfacing the detail unprompted in late 2025, nearly
three decades after the 1998 funeral, is the same signal the search data
shows: Alex's work and the Morley story are a recurring, low-intensity
touchstone.

Lineage is anchored in the ancestry tree
(`raw/self/ancestry/extracted/Daniel Frank family tree.txt`), which
records Morley Jay Frank with a Find a Grave memorial (#201542137) —
confirming the paternal placement the prior summary had left open.

**Gaps:** whether Alex's funeral essay was published somewhere findable or
shared privately within the family; any direct relationship or contact
between Dan and Alex beyond reading his work. (The family branch is
confirmed paternal via the Frank surname — both Alex's account above and
the ancestry tree place Uncle Morley and Sis squarely in the Frank line.)

## Open lead — "pops", 2018 (added 2026-09-04)

`infobox.relationship_to_dan` on this page is `unknown`, and this page's
`sources:` do not include the twitter archive. The archive holds one address to
`@alexgfrank`:

> *"@alexgfrank tough week. hang in there pops"* — 2018-09-08T02:47:40

Surfaced while ingesting [[wiki/self/twitter/replies]], which is where the
crosslink debt was found rather than the finding. **This is a lead and not a
settlement:** "pops" is used loosely enough in Dan's register that it cannot
carry a relationship on its own, and one tweet with no thread around it fixes
neither generation nor household. What it does establish is that the two
accounts were in contact in September 2018 and that something was wrong that
week — which is more than this page held before.

**What would settle it:** the Ancestry tree already cited here naming an Alex,
or a contacts export resolving `@alexgfrank`. Neither is in `raw/` today.

re-engaging with Alex's byline and career, consistent with ordinary
proud-cousin interest rather than anything more active in the
relationship.
**Gaps:** exact family branch (which side connects him to Dan — likely
paternal, via the Frank surname, but not confirmed); whether the funeral
essay was published somewhere findable or shared privately within the
